body.en: Pre-calculus functions form the cornerstone of ACT Math Level 1. Questions evaluate rational function behaviors, vertical/horizontal/slant asymptotes, domain restrictions, composition chains, and algebraic inverses.

label.en: Definition 3.1 — Function Inverses, Domain Restrictions, and Symmetries

body.en:
Fundamental properties of mappings and functions:
  • One-to-One and Invertibility: A function \(f: X \to Y\) is one-to-one (injective) if \(f(x_1) = f(x_2) \implies x_1 = x_2\) (passes the Horizontal Line Test). Its inverse \(f^{-1}\) satisfies:
    \[ (f \circ f^{-1})(x) = x \quad \text{and} \quad (f^{-1} \circ f)(x) = x \]\[ \text{Domain}(f^{-1}) = \text{Range}(f), \qquad \text{Range}(f^{-1}) = \text{Domain}(f) \]The graph of \(y = f^{-1}(x)\) is the reflection of \(y = f(x)\) across the line \(y = x\).
  • Even and Odd Symmetries:
    Even Function: \(f(-x) = f(x)\) for all \(x\) (symmetric about the \(y\)-axis, e.g., \(x^2, \cos x\)).
    Odd Function: \(f(-x) = -f(x)\) for all \(x\) (rotational symmetry of \(180^\circ\) about origin, e.g., \(x^3, \sin x\)).

label.en: Theorem 3.1 — Asymptotic Classification of Rational Functions

body.en:
For \(f(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = \frac{a_n x^n + \dots + a_0}{b_m x^m + \dots + b_0}\) reduced to lowest terms:
  • Vertical Asymptotes & Holes:
    If \((x - c)\) divides both \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\), \(x = c\) is a removable discontinuity (hole) at \(\left(c, \lim_{x \to c} f(x)\right)\).
    If \(Q(c) = 0\) and \(P(c) \neq 0\), the line \(x = c\) is a vertical asymptote.
  • Horizontal & Slant Asymptotes:
    If \(n < m\): Horizontal asymptote is \(y = 0\) (the \(x\)-axis).
    If \(n = m\): Horizontal asymptote is \(y = \frac{a_n}{b_m}\) (ratio of leading coefficients).
    If \(n = m + 1\): Slant (oblique) asymptote \(y = mx + b\) obtained by polynomial long division \(P(x) = Q(x)(mx + b) + R(x)\).
    If \(n > m + 1\): No linear asymptote (end behavior dominated by polynomial quotient).

label.en: ▲ ACT Math 2 Traps & Pitfalls — Rational, Piecewise & Inverse Functions

body.en:
• Holes vs. Vertical Asymptotes: If a factor cancels from both numerator and denominator, it creates a removable hole \((c, y_0)\), NOT a vertical asymptote. A vertical asymptote occurs ONLY where the reduced denominator equals zero.
  • Piecewise Boundary Conditions: When evaluating piecewise functions at domain boundaries (e.g. \(x = 0\)), check the inequality symbols carefully (\(<\) vs. \(\le\)) to apply the correct rule.
  • Inverse Function Domain & Range Swap: The domain of \(f^{-1}\) is the range of \(f\), and the range of \(f^{-1}\) is the domain of \(f\). A function only has an inverse function if it is strictly one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test).
  • Composite Function Order: \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\) means evaluate \(g(x)\) first, then substitute that output into \(f\). In general, \(f(g(x)) \neq g(f(x))\).

label.en: ◆ Why It Works — First-Principles Derivation (Advanced Functions)

body.en:
Why Completing the Square & Log-Linearization Work: Any quadratic \(f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c\) (\(a \ne 0\)) can be rewritten by factoring \(a\) from the first two terms and adding/subtracting \((b/2a)^2\):

\[ ax^2 + bx + c = a\!\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 + \left(c - \frac{b^2}{4a}\right) \]

Because \(\left(x + \frac{b}{2a}\right)^2 \ge 0\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), the extreme value \(k = c - \frac{b^2}{4a}\) is attained uniquely at the axis of symmetry \(x = -\frac{b}{2a}\), restricting the range to \([k, \infty)\) (if \(a > 0\)) and making \(f\) invertible on \(x \ge -\frac{b}{2a}\). Similarly, applying \(\ln\) to power laws \(y = ax^n\) yields \(\ln y = n\ln x + \ln a\), transforming a nonlinear curve into a straight line of gradient \(n\).

label.en: Worked Example 3.A — Slant Asymptote via Polynomial Long Division

body.en:
Find the equation of the slant (oblique) asymptote for \(f(x) = \dfrac{2x^2 + 5x - 3}{x + 1}\).

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Verify the degrees: Numerator degree is 2, denominator degree is 1. Since \(2 = 1 + 1\), a slant asymptote exists.
  2. Perform polynomial division \((2x^2 + 5x - 3) \div (x + 1)\):
    \[ 2x^2 \div x = 2x \]\[ (2x)(x + 1) = 2x^2 + 2x \]\[ (2x^2 + 5x - 3) - (2x^2 + 2x) = 3x - 3 \]\[ 3x \div x = 3 \]\[ 3(x + 1) = 3x + 3 \]\[ (3x - 3) - (3x + 3) = -6 \text{ (remainder)} \]
  3. Write in quotient-remainder form:
    \[ f(x) = 2x + 3 - \frac{6}{x + 1} \]
  4. As \(x \to \pm\infty\), \(\frac{6}{x + 1} \to 0\), so \(f(x) \to 2x + 3\).
The slant asymptote is the straight line \(\mathbf{y = 2x + 3}\).

label.en: Worked Example 3.B — Algebraic Inversion and Domain Specification

body.en:
Given \(f(x) = \dfrac{3x + 4}{x - 2}\) for \(x eq 2\):
(a) Find the inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\).
(b) State the domain and range of \(f^{-1}(x)\).

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Set \(y = rac{3x + 4}{x - 2}\) and swap variables to solve for \(y\):
    \[ x = rac{3y + 4}{y - 2} \implies x(y - 2) = 3y + 4 \]\[ xy - 2x = 3y + 4 \implies xy - 3y = 2x + 4 \]\[ y(x - 3) = 2x + 4 \implies y = rac{2x + 4}{x - 3} \]
  2. Thus, the inverse function is \(f^{-1}(x) = \mathbf{ rac{2x + 4}{x - 3}}\).
  3. For \(f(x)\): Domain is \(x eq 2\); Horizontal asymptote is \(y = 3\), so Range is \(y eq 3\).
  4. By domain-range duality:
    \( ext{Domain}(f^{-1}) = ext{Range}(f) = \mathbf{\{x \in \mathbb{R} \mid x eq 3\}}\).
    \( ext{Range}(f^{-1}) = ext{Domain}(f) = \mathbf{\{y \in \mathbb{R} \mid y eq 2\}}\).

Problem (Easy): The functions \( f \) and \( g \) are defined for all real numbers by \[ f(x) = 2x^2 - 3 \] and \[ g(x) = 3x + 1 \] What is the value of \( f(g(-2)) \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: To find the composite value \( f(g(-2)) \), evaluate the inner function first, then substitute the result into the outer function: 1. Evaluate \( g(-2) \): \[ g(-2) = 3(-2) + 1 = -6 + 1 = -5 \] 2. Substitute \(-5\) into \( f(x) \): \[ f(-5) = 2(-5)^2 - 3 = 2(25) - 3 = 50 - 3 = 47 \] Common Errors: - Evaluating \( g(f(-2)) \) reverses the composition order, yielding \( f(-2) = 2(4) - 3 = 5 \) and \( g(5) = 3(5) + 1 = 16 \). - Omitting parentheses when squaring \(-5\) leads to \(-25\), giving \( 2(-25) - 3 = -53 \).

Problem (Medium): The function \( f \) is defined by \[ f(x) = \frac{ax + 8}{cx + d} \] for all real numbers \( x \neq -\frac{d}{c} \), where \( a \), \( c \), and \( d \) are nonzero constants. In the standard \((x, y)\) coordinate plane, the graph of \( y = f(x) \) has a horizontal asymptote at \( y = 2 \), a vertical asymptote at \( x = 3 \), and an \( x \)-intercept at \((-4, 0)\). What is the value of \( f^{-1}(4) \)?

Step-by-Step Solution: We determine the constants \( a \), \( c \), and \( d \) step-by-step: 1. **Use the \( x \)-intercept:** The point \((-4, 0)\) lies on the graph, meaning \( f(-4) = 0 \). For a rational function, the numerator must equal zero at an \( x \)-intercept: \[ a(-4) + 8 = 0 \implies -4a = -8 \implies a = 2 \] 2. **Use the horizontal asymptote:** For \( f(x) = \frac{ax + 8}{cx + d} \), as \( x \to \pm\infty \), the horizontal asymptote is given by the ratio of the leading coefficients: \[ y = \frac{a}{c} = 2 \] Since \( a = 2 \), we have \( \frac{2}{c} = 2 \implies c = 1 \). 3. **Use the vertical asymptote:** A vertical asymptote occurs where the denominator is zero (and the numerator is nonzero). Given the asymptote is \( x = 3 \): \[ c(3) + d = 0 \implies 1(3) + d = 0 \implies d = -3 \] Checking the numerator at \( x = 3 \): \( 2(3) + 8 = 14 \neq 0 \), so \( x = 3 \) is confirmed as a vertical asymptote. Thus, the function is: \[ f(x) = \frac{2x + 8}{x - 3} \] 4. **Find \( f^{-1}(4) \):** Let \( x = f^{-1}(4) \), which means \( f(x) = 4 \): \[ \frac{2x + 8}{x - 3} = 4 \] \[ 2x + 8 = 4(x - 3) \] \[ 2x + 8 = 4x - 12 \] \[ 20 = 2x \implies x = 10 \] **Common Misconceptions:** - Calculating \( f(4) \) instead of \( f^{-1}(4) \) gives \( \frac{2(4)+8}{4-3} = 16 \). - Making a sign error with the vertical asymptote factor (using \( x + 3 \) instead of \( x - 3 \)) gives \( \frac{2x+8}{x+3} = 4 \implies x = -2 \). - Reversing the sign of the \( x \)-intercept (using \((4, 0)\)) gives \( a = -2 \) and \( c = -1 \), resulting in \( x = 2 \).

caption.en: Error Diagnosis — Common Student Traps vs. Exam-Board Method (Advanced Functions)

rows.en: Confuses the product law \(\ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y\) with a non-existent sum rule.
Only factor products, quotients, and powers inside logarithms: \(\ln(xy) = \ln x + \ln y\).
Keeping both roots of \(\sqrt{2x+6} = x - 1\) without checking \(x - 1 \ge 0\)
Squaring both sides loses the sign of \(x - {r}\), introducing roots where \(\sqrt{\cdot} = -\text{number}\).
Enforce the range condition \(x \ge 1\) before or after squaring.
Restricting domain of \(f(x) = (x-3)^2 + 1\) to \(x \ge 0\) for invertibility
The vertex is at \(x = 3\), so \(f(2) = f(4) = 2\) fails the horizontal line test on \(x \ge 0\).
Restrict the domain at the vertex axis of symmetry: \(x \ge 3\) (or \(x \le 3\)).

label.en: ▲ Exam Pacing & Verification Strategy — Advanced Functions

body.en: Fast Exam Check (ACT International Subject Test — Math 1): To verify an inverse function \(f^{-1}(x)\) in 5 seconds, pick a simple input \(x_0\), compute \(y_0 = f(x_0)\), and check that \(f^{-1}(y_0) = x_0\). Also verify that the graph of \(y = f^{-1}(x)\) reflects \(y = f(x)\) across \(y = x\).

question.en: A function is defined piecewise: \(f(x) = x^2\) for \(x < 0\), and \(f(x) = 2x+1\) for \(x \geq 0\). What is the value of \(f(-3) + f(2)\)?

solution.en:
Evaluate each term according to its interval condition:
For \(x = -3 < 0\): \(f(-3) = (-3)^2 = 9\).
For \(x = 2 \geq 0\): \(f(2) = 2(2) + 1 = 5\).
Sum: \(f(-3) + f(2) = 9 + 5 = \mathbf{14}\).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Advanced Functions and start from \(f(x) = x^2\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(x = -3 < 0\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: Let \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 - 5x + 6}\). Identify the locations of all vertical asymptotes and removable discontinuities (holes) of \(f(x)\).

solution.en:
Factor numerator and denominator completely:
\[ f(x) = \frac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(x - 2)(x - 3)} \]
Notice that \((x - 3)\) is a common factor in both numerator and denominator:
  • Removable Discontinuity (Hole): Occurs at \(x = 3\). To find the \(y\)-coordinate, evaluate the simplified fraction: \(f_{\text{reduced}}(3) = \frac{3 + 3}{3 - 2} = \frac{6}{1} = 6\). The hole is at \(\mathbf{(3, 6)}\).
  • Vertical Asymptote: The remaining uncancelled denominator factor is \(x - 2 = 0\), creating a vertical asymptote at line \(\mathbf{x = 2}\).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Advanced Functions and start from \(f(x) = \dfrac{x^2 - 9}{x^2 - 5x + 6}\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \( f(x) = \frac{(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(x - 2)(x - 3)} \).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: Determine whether the function \(g(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{x^2 + 4}\) is even, odd, or neither.

solution.en:
Evaluate \(g(-x)\) by substituting \(-x\) for every occurrence of \(x\):
\[ g(-x) = \frac{(-x)^3}{(-x)^2 + 4} = \frac{-x^3}{x^2 + 4} = -\left(\frac{x^3}{x^2 + 4}\right) = -g(x) \]
Because \(g(-x) = -g(x)\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), \(g(x)\) is an odd function (symmetric with respect to \(180^\circ\) rotation about the origin).

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Advanced Functions and start from \(g(x) = \dfrac{x^3}{x^2 + 4}\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \(g(-x)\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.

question.en: If \(f(x) = 2x - 5\) and \(g(x) = x^2 + 3\), find the expression for \((f \circ g)(x)\) and solve for all \(x\) such that \((f \circ g)(x) = 25\).

solution.en:
Step 1: Form the composite function \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\):
\[ f(g(x)) = f(x^2 + 3) = 2(x^2 + 3) - 5 = 2x^2 + 6 - 5 = \mathbf{2x^2 + 1} \]

Step 2: Solve \(2x^2 + 1 = 25\):
\[ 2x^2 = 24 \implies x^2 = 12 \implies x = \pm \sqrt{12} = \mathbf{\pm 2\sqrt{3}} \]

hints.en: Tier 1 (Conceptual Setup): Identify the governing relationship in Advanced Functions and start from \(f(x) = 2x - 5\).
Tier 2 (Key Transformation): Apply the key algebraic/geometric step leading toward \((f \circ g)(x) = f(g(x))\).
Tier 3 (Final Verification): Check signs, units, and domain restrictions on your result before opening the full solution below.
